title: Annotations on the Definitive Guide to the Western Land
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: This book (The Definitive Guide to the Western Land) is a record of the instructions of the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing. Having come from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whatever he spoke was the essential mystery of practice. If one can contemplate it constantly and strive to follow it, one will surely be reborn in the highest grade.

inline.s: Spoken by the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing
Compiled by the bodhisattva-precept disciple Chang She
This is no small karmic bond; you should cherish it as a rare and hard-to-meet chance,
the Western Land is vast beyond measure; a single thought of faith is enough to reach it.
This book
(The Definitive Guide to the Western Land)

is a record of the instructions of the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing. Having come from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whatever he spoke was the essential mystery of practice. If one can contemplate it from time to time and strive to follow it, one will surely be reborn in the highest grade.
[Definitive Guide to the West] This is an exact indication: to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is the genuine path of practice.

blocks.text: Preface to The Definitive Guide to the Western Land

inline.s: [In the summer of the year Ding-wei, I called at the abbot's quarters of Master Xueshan. He brought out a book and gave it to me, saying: 'This is a precious raft, and its origins are most extraordinary.']
In the summer of the year Ding-wei (
), I (the author of this preface) called at the abbot's quarters of Master Xueshan. He brought out a book and handed it to me, saying
This is a precious boat for crossing the bitter sea of birth and death! And its origins are most extraordinary."
[At the end of the Ming dynasty, eight friends of Wucheng practiced together the way of the mystics, daily inviting the planchette immortals to discuss their arts. When it came to the last
zú
at the end)
a spirit came, and what it spoke differed from all the other immortals. So they served it every day and grew most familiar
xiá
intimate)

with it. After a long while, it suddenly urged them to recite the Buddha's name. They asked: 'Can reciting the Buddha's name lead to the Way?' It replied: 'It is the very method.' They all recited: 'Namo Buddha.' It said: 'It is not to be recited that way.' They asked how it should be done. It said: 'You must join your palms and, with utmost sincerity, bow toward the West and recite: "Namo Amitābha Buddha."' They followed it. It then explained to them in fine detail the practice of Buddha-recitation, bidding them to cast off the false and return to the true, and to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. It then began to reveal its past causes, the Bodhisattva's name, and manifested rare fragrances and heavenly flowers and every kind of auspicious sign. And these eight, all of them, turned from their wrong practices and returned to right faith.]

Toward the end of the Ming dynasty, eight friends of Wucheng (present-day Wu County of Jiangsu Province, under Suzhou City) practiced together the way of the mystics, daily setting up the planchette and inviting the immortals, discoursing on the arts of immortal cultivation. At last, a spirit descended with a message, and what it spoke was very different from the other immortals. So they waited on it daily and sought its instruction, growing ever more familiar and convinced. After a long while, the spirit suddenly urged them to recite the Buddha's name. They asked: 'Can reciting the Buddha's name bring one to the Way?' It answered: 'It is the wondrous method for attaining the Way.' They all recited together: 'Namo Buddha.' The spirit said: 'It is not to be recited that way.' They asked: 'How, then, is it to be recited?' It said: 'You must join your palms and, with your most sincere heart, bow toward the West, and recite: "Namo Amitābha Buddha."' They followed its instruction and bowed to Amitābha Buddha. Thereupon the spirit gave them a detailed and subtle exposition of the practice of Buddha-recitation, bidding them to cast off the false and return to the true, and to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. It also began to reveal the causes of a past life (eight hundred years earlier the Bodhisattva had been their teacher), its own Bodhisattva title (the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing), and manifested rare fragrances and heavenly flowers, and all manner of auspicious signs. And these eight all renounced their wrong practices and returned to right faith.
[Planchette (
jī

)] A method of divination, also called 'the phoenix basket,' 'the lowered brush,' 'inviting the immortals,' and other names. In planchette divination, one person plays the role of one possessed by a deity; such a person is called a luan-sheng. The deity then possesses the luan-sheng and writes characters to convey its instruction (an oracle). Through this means the faithful communicate with the deity. [Phoenix (luan)] The phoenix-luan is a mythical bird of ancient China, the messenger of Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West, responsible for bringing tidings from the deities. Thus 'phoenix' also carries the meaning of conveying a divine message. [Utmost sincerity (zhi xin)] The most sincere heart.
[Wuxiu, the teacher of the eight, was the leader among them. The Bodhisattva bade him go to Master Sanmei to receive the vinaya
(receive the precepts)
and perfect the form of a monk. At first the master made it difficult for him; but when he saw the Bodhisattva's 'Moon Gatha,' he bowed toward the West and had him shaved. This was because
(this was because)

when the Bodhisattva first came, the gathering took him for an immortal and, taking the moon as the theme, asked for a verse. He then gave them this gatha: 'One moon's light holds a thousand worlds; countless bodies shine on the deluded. Know that the essence is originally one; motionless, majestic, it is the working of change.']

Wuxiu was the teacher among the eight. The Bodhisattva sent him to Master Sanmei to be shaved and receive the precepts, so as to perfect the form of a monk. At first Master Sanmei made it difficult for him (at first, seeing that Wuxiu had come with an oracle from the planchette altar, he thought the gods and spirits had sent him, and refused to shave his head or give him the precepts); later, when he saw the 'Moon Gatha' shown by the Bodhisattva, he knew this was the command of a great Bodhisattva come from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so bowed toward the West and had him shaved. This was because, when the Bodhisattva first came to the planchette altar, the gathering thought he was an immortal, and took the moon as the theme to request a verse. The Bodhisattva therefore spoke this gatha:
'A single moon
(the Bodhisattva's reward-body)
shines
(the Bodhisattva's emanation-body)
over
(encompassing)
a thousand worlds
(the three thousand great chiliocosms)
, countless bodies shine on the deluded
(sending forth countless emanation-bodies to save the countless deluded and upside-down beings)
, know that the essence is originally one
(should understand that the Bodhisattva's reward-body is always just this one)
, motionless, majestic, the working of change

(though with countless emanation-bodies it responds to occasion and saves countless beings throughout the three thousand great chiliocosms, its reward-body in the Land of Ultimate Bliss remains ever still and unmoving)
[Master Sanmei] That is the famous Lawyer Sanmei (for details see
A Dream of Wandering

). All his life he propagated the vinaya, knew in advance the time of his coming and going, and passed away at a set time while seated. On the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month of the first year of Hongguang of the Ming dynasty (

) Master Sanmei returned from Suzhou to Bao Hua Mountain in Nanjing, and the assembly bowed to him and asked after his health. The master smiled and said: 'Today I make an appointment with you (I tell you in advance now): between three days and seven days from now, will I not be free from the hanging? (I will be reborn freely; the original text means: can I not be reborn freely?)' Hearing this the assembly all wept in sorrow. The master said: 'Birth and death are but an illusion; in truth there is no coming and going. Why do you weep?' When the first day of the month came, the master looked over the almanac and said: 'At the si hour of the fourth day (in the morning from

o'clock) I will enter nirvāṇa!' Thereupon in the abbot's room he rang the wooden gong and gathered the assembly, transmitted the Dharma to Lawyer Jianyue (the author of A Dream of Wandering), entrusted him with the affairs of the monastery, and settled the matters of his own passing. When the fourth day came he gathered the assembly again, drew water and bathed. He then taught: 'When the water dries up I will go. Do not think in terms of coming or going; you must not wear mourning or weep, you must not send word of my passing far and wide — cast aside all worldly rites, every one of them. After three days bury me on Dragon Mountain of the monastery.' He then bade the assembly recite the Buddha's name; when the water had dried up he sat cross-legged, smiled, and passed away. The monastery only recited the scriptures with utmost sincerity for three days, and held no worldly ceremonies at all.
[Suspended release (xuan jie)]

To be freed from being hung upside down: delivered from a state of distress. [Three bodies] The Dharma-body, the reward-body, and the emanation-body. The Dharma-body is the ever-abiding, unperishing true nature that all beings inherently possess; only sentient beings are deluded and do not reveal it, while buddhas and bodhisattvas are awakened and realize it. The reward-body is the body accomplished through the wisdom and merit of a buddha or bodhisattva. The emanation-body is the body that a buddha or bodhisattva manifests in response to the capacities and circumstances of sentient beings.
[It began on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month of the year Gui-wei of Chongzhen of the Ming, and lasted until
qì
ended at)

the second day of the tenth month of the year Ding-hai of Shunzhi of the Qing — twenty-four assemblies in all. What was spoken was all the essential mystery of practice; and because the gatha contained the line 'definitively pointing out the correct path of practice,' the record was therefore named The Definitive Guide to the Western Land.]
The Bodhisattva's exposition of the practice of Buddha-recitation began on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month of the year Gui-wei of Chongzhen of the Ming (
) and ended on the second day of the tenth month of the year Ding-hai of Shunzhi of the Qing (

) — twenty-four assemblies in all. What was spoken was all the essential mystery of practice; and because the gatha the Bodhisattva spoke contained the line 'definitively pointing out the correct path of practice,' this record of instructions was therefore titled The Definitive Guide to the Western Land.
The above was spoken by Master Xueshan.
[When I read it, my body and mind leapt with joy, no less than
bù chì,
as though)

sweet ambrosia dripping into a parched heart! So I could not cease exclaiming at its wonder. Master Xueshan said: 'At first I too did not believe it; but after I had read it, my spirit shone forth, and even were I to try I could not disbelieve.' I said: 'In the past, in his causal ground, the Bodhisattva had a great affinity with these eight; because his compassionate remembrance was deep, he used skillful means to come to the planchette and guide them. How can this be compared with the company of those who respond through the planchette! Moreover, in his parting instructions the Bodhisattva said: "The planchette is established as a support for spirits and ghosts; it is not the constant work of a great Bodhisattva's transformational response." So how can this book be regarded as an ordinary planchette text?'

After reading it, I (the author of this preface) leapt with joy in body and mind, like sweet ambrosia dripping into a withered heart! So I could not stop exclaiming at its wonder. Master Xueshan said: 'At first I did not believe it either; but after I had finished reading it, my spirit shone forth, and even if I wanted to disbelieve I could not.' I said: 'In the past, in his causal ground, the Bodhisattva had a great affinity with these eight; because his compassionate remembrance was deep, he therefore used skillful means to come to the planchette and guide them. How can this be lumped together with the spirits and ghosts of the planchette! Moreover, in his parting instructions the Bodhisattva said: "The planchette is in itself a support for spirits and ghosts; it is not the constant work of a great Bodhisattva responding to occasion to save beings." So how can this book be looked upon as an ordinary planchette text?'

[At that time I at once wished to print it and circulate it, to benefit the many widely, but the causes were not yet joined. Up to now, in the spring of the year Ji-you, monks, laypeople, and fellow practitioners of the Way one and all leapt with joy and wished to contribute funds
(zī, the same as 'zi')

to help bring it to completion. There were even some who, reading it, wept, and weeping read on, abruptly giving up their beloved houses, clothes, and implements to go into the deep mountains and recite the Buddha's name. Is this not the great compassion without conditions, gathering and transforming sentient beings — a matter beyond thought? Thereupon I consulted with the two teachers Lingxi and Huiji, planning to have it printed. When the printing blocks
(zǐ, the carved blocks for printing)
were completed, I have related its whole course as such.]
At that time I at once wished to carve blocks and print the book for circulation, so as to benefit beings widely, but the causes were not yet complete. Up to now, in the spring of the year Ji-you (

), monks, laypeople, and fellow practitioners of the Way one and all leapt with joy and were willing to contribute funds to help print it. There were even some who, reading it, wept, and weeping read on, abruptly giving up their beloved houses, clothes, and implements to go into the deep mountains and recite the Buddha's name. Is this not the Bodhisattva's great compassion without conditions, gathering and transforming sentient beings — a matter beyond thought? Thereupon I consulted with the two teachers Lingxi and Huiji, and we planned to carve the blocks and print it. When the printing was finished, I have recorded the whole course of the matter as such.
[At that time, in the year Ji-you of Kangxi, on the sixteenth day of the ninth month
(the day after the full moon, that is, the sixteenth day of the lunar month)
, composed by Jin E, styled Langxi, a Pure-Land practitioner of ancient Wu.]
In the year Ji-you of Kangxi (
), on the sixteenth day of the ninth month, the Pure-Land practitioner of Wucheng, Jin E, styled Langxi, wrote this preface.

blocks.text: Postface to The Definitive Guide to the Western Land

inline.s: [The sages and holy men of antiquity are far removed from us today. Yet when we read their books and know their words, we may be certain they cannot have been forged; the judgment rests on principle alone. Since the Buddha's Dharma entered China, in these fifteen hundred years the heroic and clear-sighted ones who obtained a single scripture or a single verse, and with decisive faith entered and transcended birth and death, have been
(dài, nearly)
beyond counting. But shallow-witted people
(zhé, then)
peep at them with their own private opinions, saying they originate from Laozi and Zhuangzi
(Laozi and Zhuangzi)
and are forgeries made by their followers. Now the books of Laozi and Zhuangzi are here before us; take them and compare them with the Shurangama Sutra
the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra and the other scriptures
(to compare)
and the reason for their shallowness or depth, their agreement or divergence, is entirely
(wholly)
plain. If Laozi and Zhuangzi could not produce such works, can those who study Laozi and Zhuangzi produce them? This is the fault of those who cannot discern principle and indulge
(xùn, to follow crookedly)
their own private inclinations.]

The sages and holy men of antiquity are far removed from us now. Yet when we read their books and understand the principles they set forth, we may be certain that they cannot have been forged, because the judgment can be made on the basis of the principles spoken of in the books. Since the Buddha's Dharma came into China, in these fifteen hundred years the heroic and clear-sighted ones who obtained a single scripture or a single verse, and with decisive faith entered and transcended birth and death, are nearly beyond counting. But shallow-witted people peer at the Buddhist scriptures with their own private opinions, saying they originate from Laozi and Zhuangzi and are forgeries made by their disciples and their disciples' disciples. Now the books of Laozi and Zhuangzi are all here; compare them with the Shurangama Sutra, the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra and the other scriptures, and the shallowness or depth, the agreement or divergence, of the two is entirely clear. If Laozi and Zhuangzi could not write books such as the Shurangama Sutra and the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, could their disciples and their disciples' disciples write them? Those who say the Buddhist scriptures come from the hands of the disciples of Laozi and Zhuangzi are people who cannot discern the principles spoken of in the books, but follow their own private inclinations and talk recklessly!
[In recent ages the practice of the flying phoenix has prevailed; the sages and holy men of the three teachings
(Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism)

often respond according to the circumstances, spreading the Dharma and saving people — all out of an unwilling heart. When we read their books and know their words, we may be certain they cannot have been forged; here too the judgment rests on principle alone.]

In recent ages the work of the planchette has been practiced, and the sages of the three teachings (Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism) often respond according to circumstances, spreading the Dharma and saving people — all out of an unwilling heart (for because the planchette was then in vogue, the Bodhisattva had no choice but to come to the altar and deliver an oracle to save beings; this is walking in a non-path so as to reach the Buddha-path). Yet when we read the planchette texts they have written out, we know that the principles they speak of cannot have been forged, also because the principles spoken of in the planchette text can be used to judge whether it is the Bodhisattva's own speech or that of a spirit or ghost.
[At that time the planchette was in full vogue.]

The Ming dynasty honored Daoism, and the planchette came out of the Daoist school, so it was also highly regarded by those in high places, flourishing among the scholar-officials, and the middle and lower classes vied to imitate it; it flourished for a time, and continued without decline down to the Qing dynasty.

[The Definitive Guide to the Western Land is the Dharma spoken by the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing in the realm of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. As a teaching it condemns wrong practices and points back to the Pure Land, expounds the wondrous truth of the one mind, and exhausts the mysterious gate of the upward path — truly a guide for those who study Buddhism.]

The book The Definitive Guide to the Western Land is the Dharma spoken by the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. His instructions condemn wrong practices and point back to the Pure Land, clarify the wondrous truth of the one mind, and exhaust the mysterious gate of the upward path — this truly is a guide for those who study Buddhism!
[The wondrous truth of the one mind.] "

One mind has the one-mindedness of practice (shi) and the one-mindedness of principle (li): without any other thought is the one-mindedness of practice (shi); entering into true reality is the one-mindedness of principle (li). 'Wondrous truth' means the subtle and exquisite true principle. 'Truth' means the reality that is not empty and not false.
[The mysterious gate of the upward path.] The utmost limit of the Chan (Zen) school is called 'the one road upward.' 'The mysterious gate of the upward path' is the doorway of that one road upward.
[I read it over and over, rose up
(arose)

and sighed: Alas! The land of the lotus flower is never apart from this very place; Amitābha Buddha is wholly within sentient beings. But these sentient beings do not know it in their daily use, and have never so much as aroused a single thought of dedication; so they go from delusion into delusion, drifting through long eons — is this not pitiful! The Bodhisattva's compassionate vow is deep and weighty; age after age he follows these beings, never abandoning them.]

I read it over and over, rose, and exclaimed: Alas! The land of the lotus is never apart from this very place; Amitābha Buddha is wholly within sentient beings. But these beings, using it daily, do not know it, and have never aroused so much as a single thought of dedication; so they go from delusion into delusion, drifting through long eons — is this not pitiful! The Bodhisattva's compassionate vow is deep and weighty; age after age he follows these beings and never abandons them in saving them.
[The land of the lotus is never apart from this very place; Amitābha Buddha is wholly within sentient beings.]
The Three-Periods Chant of Master Zhongfeng says:

Amitābha Buddha is my very mind, my own mind is Amitābha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, this very place is the Pure Land. Is it not that delusion and awakening differ on their own — how could there be a holy and a common, an other and a self?'

[How does the transformation of the flying phoenix differ from manifesting a body to teach the Dharma? One who reads this book and truly believes his own fundamental mind, practices as it teaches, and dedicates thought after thought, with no other distracting thought, until thought reaches its limit and emotion is emptied, freed and dwelling nowhere — though now dwelling in the five turbidities of the evil world, already his whole body sits within the lotus land. When the retribution of this body's conditions ends, in the snapping of a finger he is reborn there. This is fruit and this is cause, with no first and no last between them. But if one does not believe his own mind, and therefore does not believe in the Pure Land, and worse still suspects this book to be a forgery, then I can do nothing with him!]

How does the transformation of the planchette differ from manifesting a body to teach the Dharma? One who reads The Definitive Guide to the Western Land and truly believes his own fundamental mind, practices as it teaches, and dedicates thought after thought, with no distracting thought, until thought reaches its limit and emotion is emptied, freed and dwelling nowhere — though now dwelling in the five turbidities of the evil world, already his whole body sits within the lotus land. When the conditions of this body's retribution come to an end, in the snapping of a finger he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is fruit and this is cause, with no first and no last between them. But if one does not believe his own mind, and therefore does not believe in the Pure Land, and even suspects this book to be a forgery, then I have no way with him!
[Five turbidities.]

First, the turbidity of the age: the age meets with evil fortune and disasters arise again and again. Second, the turbidity of afflictions: people's hearts are filled with the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion. Third, the turbidity of beings: beings' faculties are lowly, with much suffering and little joy. Fourth, the turbidity of views: wrong views prevail and thought is confused. Fifth, the turbidity of life: sentient beings, retributed by evil karma, are worn in body and mind, and their lives are short.
[Retribution-conditions (bao yuan).]
The causes and conditions of retribution. Here it refers to the lifespan of this one lifetime.
[To have no recourse (mo ru zhi he).] To have no way
out, utterly helpless.
[This book I obtained from my friend Wang Guansan; there had been printing blocks, but recently
(not long ago)
they were destroyed by fire. My fellow villagers

(the worthies) will have it carved anew to circulate in the world. I have respectfully corrected its chapters and sentences, and set them in order. When it was done, I have written this preface as such.]

This book (The Definitive Guide to the Western Land) I obtained from my friend Wang Guansan; there had been printing blocks, but not long ago they were destroyed in a fire. My fellow villagers, the worthies, will have it carved anew and printed, so that it may circulate in the world. I respectfully corrected its chapters and sentences, and set them in order. The book being done, I have related the matter thus.
